law_text: GDPR Article 1 - Subject-matter and objectives: This Regulation lays down rules relating to the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and rules relating to the free movement of personal data. It protects fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons, in particular their right to the protection of personal data.

GDPR Article 2 - Material scope: This Regulation applies to the processing of personal data wholly or partly by automated means and to the processing other than by automated means of personal data which form part of a filing system. It does not apply to purely personal or household activities.

GDPR Article 3 - Territorial scope: This Regulation applies to the processing of personal data in the context of the activities of an establishment of a controller or a processor in the Union, regardless of whether the processing takes place in the Union or not. It also applies to controllers outside the EU offering goods or services to EU data subjects.

GDPR Article 4(1) - Definition of Personal Data: Personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person. An identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, ID number, location data, or online identifier.

GDPR Article 4(2) - Definition of Processing: Processing means any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, whether or not by automated means, such as collection, recording, organisation, structuring, storage, adaptation, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure, dissemination, restriction, erasure or destruction.

GDPR Article 4(7) - Definition of Controller: Controller means the natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data. Where the purposes and means of such processing are determined by Union or Member State law, the controller may be designated by that law.

GDPR Article 4(8) - Definition of Processor: Processor means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which processes personal data on behalf of the controller. Processors must act only on documented instructions from the controller and may not engage sub-processors without prior written authorisation.

GDPR Article 4(11) - Definition of Consent: Consent of the data subject means any freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes by which he or she, by a statement or by a clear affirmative action, signifies agreement to the processing of personal data relating to him or her.

GDPR Article 5(1)(a) - Lawfulness, Fairness and Transparency: Personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject. Controllers must be able to demonstrate that processing has a legitimate legal basis and that data subjects are adequately informed.

GDPR Article 5(1)(b) - Purpose Limitation: Personal data shall be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes. Further processing for archiving, scientific, historical or statistical purposes shall not be considered incompatible.

GDPR Article 5(1)(c) - Data Minimisation: Personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed. Organisations cannot hoard user data just in case it becomes useful later.

GDPR Article 5(1)(d) - Accuracy: Personal data shall be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date. Every reasonable step must be taken to ensure that personal data that are inaccurate, having regard to the purposes for which they are processed, are erased or rectified without delay.

GDPR Article 5(1)(e) - Storage Limitation: Personal data shall be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed. Data retained for archiving, scientific, historical or statistical purposes may be kept longer if appropriate safeguards are in place.

GDPR Article 5(1)(f) - Integrity and Confidentiality: Personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.

GDPR Article 5(2) - Accountability: The controller shall be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, the principles in Article 5(1). This accountability principle requires organisations to maintain documentation, conduct impact assessments, and implement governance measures to prove lawful data handling.

GDPR Article 6(1)(a) - Lawful Basis: Consent: Processing shall be lawful only if the data subject has given consent to the processing of his or her personal data for one or more specific purposes. Consent must be freely given and is not valid if there is a clear imbalance of power between the data subject and the controller.

GDPR Article 6(1)(b) - Lawful Basis: Contract: Processing is lawful where it is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is party, or in order to take steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract. Bundling unnecessary data requests with contract requirements is not permitted.

GDPR Article 6(1)(c) - Lawful Basis: Legal Obligation: Processing is lawful where it is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject. The legal obligation must be based on Union or Member State law and must be sufficiently clear about the data processing it requires.

GDPR Article 6(1)(d) - Lawful Basis: Vital Interests: Processing is lawful where it is necessary in order to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person. This basis should only be relied on where processing cannot be clearly based on another legal basis such as consent.

GDPR Article 6(1)(e) - Lawful Basis: Public Task: Processing is lawful where it is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller. The task must be laid down by Union or Member State law.

GDPR Article 6(1)(f) - Lawful Basis: Legitimate Interests: Processing is lawful where necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or by a third party, except where such interests are overridden by the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject, in particular where the data subject is a child.

GDPR Article 7(1) - Demonstrating Consent: Where processing is based on consent, the controller shall be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to processing of his or her personal data. Organisations must keep records of when, how, and what consent was given by each data subject.

GDPR Article 7(2) - Written Consent Declaration: If the data subject's consent is given in the context of a written declaration which also concerns other matters, the request for consent shall be presented in a manner which is clearly distinguishable from the other matters. Pre-ticked boxes do not constitute valid consent.

GDPR Article 7(3) - Right to Withdraw Consent: The data subject shall have the right to withdraw his or her consent at any time. The withdrawal of consent shall not affect the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal. Withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent.

GDPR Article 7(4) - Freely Given Consent: When assessing whether consent is freely given, utmost account shall be taken of whether, inter alia, the performance of a contract, including the provision of a service, is conditional on consent to the processing of personal data that is not necessary for the performance of that contract.

GDPR Article 8 - Conditions Applicable to Child's Consent: Where processing relates to a child below 16 years of age for information society services, consent shall be given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility. Member States may provide by law for a lower age of not below 13 years for such processing.

GDPR Article 9(1) - Special Categories of Data: Processing of personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data, health data, or data concerning a natural person's sex life or sexual orientation shall be prohibited.

GDPR Article 9(2) - Exceptions to Special Categories Prohibition: The prohibition on processing special categories of data shall not apply where the data subject has given explicit consent, processing is necessary for employment obligations, or processing is necessary to protect vital interests where the data subject is incapable of giving consent.

GDPR Article 10 - Processing of Criminal Conviction Data: Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences or related security measures shall be carried out only under the control of official authority or when the processing is authorised by Union or Member State law providing for appropriate safeguards.

GDPR Article 12 - Transparent Information and Communication: The controller shall take appropriate measures to provide any information and any communication relating to processing to the data subject in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language, in particular for any information addressed specifically to a child.

GDPR Article 13(1) - Information to be Provided at Collection: Where personal data relating to a data subject are collected from the data subject, the controller shall provide the data subject with the identity and contact details of the controller, the purposes and legal basis of processing, and any legitimate interests pursued by the controller.

GDPR Article 13(2) - Additional Information at Collection: In addition to basic information, the controller shall provide the data subject with the retention period, the right to request access, rectification, erasure, or restriction, the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority, and whether provision of personal data is a statutory or contractual requirement.

GDPR Article 14 - Information When Data Not Obtained Directly: Where personal data have not been obtained from the data subject, the controller shall provide the data subject with the source of the personal data within a reasonable period and at the latest within one month of obtaining the data.

GDPR Article 15(1) - Right of Access: The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller confirmation as to whether or not personal data concerning him or her are being processed, and, where that is the case, access to the personal data and related information about the processing.

GDPR Article 15(3) - Right to Receive a Copy: The controller shall provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing. For any further copies requested by the data subject, the controller may charge a reasonable fee based on administrative costs. Where the data subject makes the request by electronic means, the information shall be provided in a commonly used electronic form.

GDPR Article 16 - Right to Rectification: The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller without undue delay the rectification of inaccurate personal data concerning him or her. Taking into account the purposes of the processing, the data subject shall have the right to have incomplete personal data completed.

GDPR Article 17 - Right to Erasure (Right to be Forgotten): The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay. A company cannot retain user data indefinitely simply for future, undefined commercial use after a user deletes their account.

GDPR Article 17(3) - Exceptions to Right to Erasure: The right to erasure shall not apply to the extent that processing is necessary for exercising the right of freedom of expression and information, for compliance with a legal obligation, for public interest in public health, for archiving purposes in the public interest, or for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims.

GDPR Article 18 - Right to Restriction of Processing: The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller restriction of processing where the accuracy of the personal data is contested, the processing is unlawful, the controller no longer needs the data, or the data subject has objected to processing.

GDPR Article 19 - Notification Obligation Regarding Rectification or Erasure: The controller shall communicate any rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing to each recipient to whom the personal data have been disclosed, unless this proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort.

GDPR Article 20 - Right to Data Portability: The data subject shall have the right to receive the personal data concerning him or her, which he or she has provided to a controller, in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and have the right to transmit those data to another controller without hindrance.

GDPR Article 20(2) - Data Portability Direct Transfer: The data subject shall have the right to have the personal data transmitted directly from one controller to another, where technically feasible. This right applies where the processing is based on consent or contract and is carried out by automated means.

GDPR Article 21(1) - Right to Object: The data subject shall have the right to object, on grounds relating to his or her particular situation, at any time to processing of personal data concerning him or her which is based on legitimate interests or public task, including profiling based on those provisions.

GDPR Article 21(2) - Right to Object to Direct Marketing: Where personal data are processed for direct marketing purposes, the data subject shall have the right to object at any time to processing of personal data concerning him or her for such marketing, including profiling to the extent that it is related to such direct marketing.

GDPR Article 21(3) - Mandatory Compliance with Direct Marketing Objection: Where the data subject objects to processing for direct marketing purposes, the personal data shall no longer be processed for such purposes. This right must be explicitly brought to the attention of the data subject and shall be presented clearly and separately from any other information.

GDPR Article 22 - Automated Individual Decision-Making Including Profiling: The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects him or her. This prohibition includes credit scoring, insurance pricing, and hiring algorithms with no human review.

GDPR Article 22(2) - Exceptions to Automated Decision-Making: Automated decisions shall be permitted where necessary for entering into or performance of a contract, authorised by Union or Member State law, or based on the data subject's explicit consent. In all cases, suitable safeguards must exist including the right to obtain human intervention.

GDPR Article 23 - Restrictions: Union or Member State law may restrict the scope of data subject rights and controller obligations where such a restriction respects the essence of fundamental rights and is a necessary and proportionate measure in a democratic society to safeguard national security, defence, or public security.

GDPR Article 24 - Responsibility of the Controller: Taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing as well as the risks of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure processing is performed in accordance with this Regulation.

GDPR Article 25(1) - Data Protection by Design: Taking into account the state of the art, the cost of implementation, and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing, the controller shall implement data-protection principles in an effective manner at the time of determining the means of processing (privacy by design).

GDPR Article 25(2) - Data Protection by Default: The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed. This applies to the amount of data collected, extent of processing, storage period, and accessibility.

GDPR Article 26 - Joint Controllers: Where two or more controllers jointly determine the purposes and means of processing, they shall be joint controllers. They shall determine their respective responsibilities for compliance with this Regulation in a transparent manner, and the data subject may exercise rights against each controller.

GDPR Article 27 - Representatives of Controllers Not Established in the Union: Where Article 3(2) applies, the controller or processor shall designate in writing a representative in the Union. The representative shall be established in one of the Member States where the data subjects are located.

GDPR Article 28(1) - Processor Obligations: Where processing is to be carried out on behalf of a controller, the controller shall use only processors providing sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures so that processing meets the requirements of this Regulation and ensures the protection of the rights of the data subject.

GDPR Article 28(3) - Data Processing Agreement: Processing by a processor shall be governed by a contract that sets out the subject-matter, duration, nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects, and the obligations and rights of the controller.

GDPR Article 29 - Processing Under Controller or Processor Authority: The processor and any person acting under the authority of the controller or of the processor who has access to personal data shall not process those data except on instructions from the controller, unless required to do so by Union or Member State law.

GDPR Article 30(1) - Records of Processing Activities: Each controller and, where applicable, the controller's representative, shall maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility. This record shall contain: name of controller, purposes of processing, categories of data subjects, categories of personal data, and planned erasure time limits.

GDPR Article 30(5) - Exemption for Small Organisations: The obligation to maintain records shall not apply to an organisation or an enterprise employing fewer than 250 persons unless the processing it carries out is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, the processing is not occasional, or it includes special categories of data.

GDPR Article 31 - Cooperation with Supervisory Authority: The controller and the processor and, where applicable, their representatives, shall cooperate, on request, with the supervisory authority in the performance of its tasks. Failure to cooperate with a supervisory authority can itself constitute a violation and lead to increased penalties.

GDPR Article 32(1) - Security of Processing: Taking into account the state of the art and the costs of implementation, controllers and processors shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including pseudonymisation, encryption, and resilience of processing systems.

GDPR Article 32(4) - Confidentiality Obligations: The controller and processor shall take steps to ensure that any natural person acting under the authority of the controller or the processor who has access to personal data does not process them except on instructions from the controller, unless required to do so by Union or Member State law.

GDPR Article 33 - Notification of a Personal Data Breach: In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority. The notification shall describe the nature of the breach, categories of data affected, and likely consequences.

GDPR Article 33(2) - Processor Breach Notification to Controller: The processor shall notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach. This notification shall assist the controller in meeting its obligation to notify supervisory authorities within the 72-hour window.

GDPR Article 34(1) - Communication of Breach to Data Subject: When the personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall communicate the personal data breach to the data subject without undue delay using clear and plain language.

GDPR Article 34(3) - Exceptions to Breach Notification to Individuals: Communication to data subjects is not required if the controller has implemented appropriate technical and organisational protection measures that render the personal data unintelligible, such as encryption, or if subsequent measures have been taken to remove the high risk.

GDPR Article 35(1) - Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA): Where a type of processing, in particular using new technologies, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall, prior to processing, carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data.

GDPR Article 35(3) - When DPIA is Required: A DPIA is required in particular in case of: systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing including profiling; processing on a large scale of special categories of data; and systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale.

GDPR Article 36 - Prior Consultation: The controller shall consult the supervisory authority prior to processing where a DPIA indicates that the processing would result in a high residual risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk. The supervisory authority must respond within eight weeks.

GDPR Article 37(1) - Designation of Data Protection Officer (DPO): The controller and the processor shall designate a data protection officer where processing is carried out by a public authority, where core activities require large-scale systematic monitoring of data subjects, or where core activities consist of large-scale processing of special category data.

GDPR Article 38 - Position of the DPO: The controller and processor shall ensure that the data protection officer is involved, properly and in a timely manner, in all issues which relate to the protection of personal data. The DPO shall not receive any instructions regarding the exercise of their tasks and shall report directly to the highest management level.

GDPR Article 39 - Tasks of the DPO: The DPO shall have the following tasks: informing and advising the controller and employees on obligations under data protection law; monitoring compliance; assigning responsibilities; providing advice on DPIAs; cooperating with the supervisory authority; and acting as the contact point for the supervisory authority.

GDPR Article 40 - Codes of Conduct: Associations and other bodies representing categories of controllers or processors may prepare codes of conduct for the purpose of specifying the application of this Regulation. Such codes shall contain mechanisms enabling the supervisory body to carry out the mandatory monitoring.

GDPR Article 42 - Certification: Member States, supervisory authorities, the Board and the Commission shall encourage, in particular at Union level, the establishment of data protection certification mechanisms and of data protection seals and marks, for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with this Regulation.

GDPR Article 44 - General Principle for Transfers: Any transfer of personal data to a third country or an international organisation shall only take place if the conditions laid down in Chapter V are complied with. All provisions of Chapter V shall be applied in order to ensure that the level of protection of natural persons guaranteed by this Regulation is not undermined.

GDPR Article 45 - Adequacy Decision Transfers: A transfer of personal data to a third country may take place where the Commission has decided that the third country ensures an adequate level of protection. Such transfers shall not require any specific authorisation, and the Commission shall monitor developments in third countries on an ongoing basis.

GDPR Article 46 - Transfers Subject to Appropriate Safeguards: In the absence of an adequacy decision, a controller or processor may transfer personal data to a third country only if the controller or processor has provided appropriate safeguards, including standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules, or approved certification mechanisms.

GDPR Article 47 - Binding Corporate Rules: Supervisory authorities shall approve binding corporate rules providing they specify the data protection principles, the rights of data subjects, acceptance of liability by the controller or processor, and the tasks of any DPO. BCRs allow multinational companies to transfer data intra-group across borders.

GDPR Article 49 - Derogations for Specific Situations: In the absence of an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards, a transfer to a third country shall only take place on conditions including explicit consent of the data subject with awareness of risks, the transfer being necessary for contract performance, or on grounds of compelling legitimate interests.

GDPR Article 51 - Supervisory Authority: Each Member State shall provide for one or more independent public authorities to be responsible for monitoring the application of this Regulation, to protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons in relation to processing and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the Union.

GDPR Article 55 - Competence of Supervisory Authorities: Each supervisory authority shall be competent for the performance of the tasks assigned to and the exercise of the powers conferred on it in accordance with this Regulation on the territory of its own Member State. The supervisory authority of the main establishment leads cross-border cases.

GDPR Article 57 - Tasks of Supervisory Authorities: Each supervisory authority shall monitor and enforce the application of this Regulation; promote public awareness; advise national institutions on legislative proposals; handle complaints from data subjects; conduct investigations; and cooperate with other supervisory authorities.

GDPR Article 58(2) - Corrective Powers: Each supervisory authority shall have the power to issue warnings to a controller or processor that intended processing operations are likely to infringe this Regulation; issue reprimands; order compliance; impose a temporary or permanent ban on processing; and impose administrative fines.

GDPR Article 60 - Cooperation Between Lead Supervisory Authority and Concerned Supervisory Authorities: The lead supervisory authority shall cooperate with the other supervisory authorities concerned in an endeavour to reach consensus. The lead supervisory authority shall communicate the relevant information and submit a draft decision to the other supervisory authorities concerned.

GDPR Article 65 - Dispute Resolution by the Board: In order to ensure the correct and consistent application of this Regulation in individual cases, the Board shall adopt a binding decision where a supervisory authority has raised an objection and the supervisory authorities cannot reach consensus, or where there are conflicting views.

GDPR Article 77 - Right to Lodge a Complaint: Without prejudice to any other administrative or judicial remedy, every data subject shall have the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority, in particular in the Member State of his or her habitual residence, place of work or place of the alleged infringement.

GDPR Article 78 - Right to an Effective Judicial Remedy Against a Supervisory Authority: Each natural or legal person shall have the right to an effective judicial remedy against a legally binding decision of a supervisory authority concerning them. Proceedings against a supervisory authority shall be brought before the courts of the Member State where the supervisory authority is established.

GDPR Article 79 - Right to an Effective Judicial Remedy Against a Controller or Processor: Each data subject shall have the right to an effective judicial remedy where he or she considers that his or her rights have been infringed as a result of the processing of his or her personal data in non-compliance with this Regulation.

GDPR Article 80 - Representation of Data Subjects: Data subjects shall have the right to mandate a not-for-profit body, organisation or association which has been properly constituted in accordance with the law of a Member State to lodge the complaint and exercise the rights referred to in Articles 77, 78 and 79 on their behalf.

GDPR Article 82(1) - Right to Compensation: Any person who has suffered material or non-material damage as a result of an infringement of this Regulation shall have the right to receive compensation from the controller or processor for the damage suffered. Non-material damage includes distress, loss of control over data, and reputational harm.

GDPR Article 82(3) - Exemption from Liability: A controller or processor shall be exempt from liability if it proves that it is not in any way responsible for the event giving rise to the damage. Demonstrating implementation of all required technical and organisational measures and following the controller's instructions may exempt processors from liability.

GDPR Article 83(1) - General Conditions for Imposing Administrative Fines: Each supervisory authority shall ensure that the imposition of administrative fines for infringements shall be effective, proportionate and dissuasive. Fines shall be imposed in addition to, or instead of, other corrective measures depending on the circumstances of each individual case.

GDPR Article 83(4) - Lower Level Fines: Infringements of obligations of the controller and the processor, obligations of the certification body, and obligations of the monitoring body shall be subject to administrative fines up to 10,000,000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 2% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year.

GDPR Article 83(5) - Higher Level Fines: Infringements of the basic principles for processing including conditions for consent, data subjects' rights, and transfers of personal data shall be subject to administrative fines up to 20,000,000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year.

GDPR Article 84 - Penalties: Member States shall lay down the rules on other penalties applicable to infringements of this Regulation, in particular for infringements which are not subject to administrative fines, and shall take all measures necessary to ensure that they are implemented. Such penalties shall be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

GDPR Article 85 - Processing and Freedom of Expression: Member States shall by law reconcile the right to the protection of personal data pursuant to this Regulation with the right to freedom of expression and information. For processing carried out for journalistic purposes or for academic, artistic or literary expression, exemptions from data protection obligations may be provided.

GDPR Article 87 - Processing of National Identification Numbers: Member States may further determine the specific conditions for the processing of a national identification number or any other identifier of general application. In that case the national identification number or any other identifier of general application shall be used only under appropriate safeguards.

GDPR Article 88 - Processing in the Context of Employment: Member States may, by law or by collective agreements, provide for more specific rules to ensure the protection of the rights and freedoms in respect of the processing of employees' personal data in the employment context, in particular for recruitment and performance assessment purposes.

GDPR Article 89 - Safeguards for Archiving, Research, and Statistical Purposes: Processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes, or statistical purposes shall be subject to appropriate safeguards. Those safeguards shall ensure that technical and organisational measures are in place, including pseudonymisation.

GDPR Recital 26 - Principles of Data Protection: The principles of data protection should apply to any information concerning an identified or identifiable natural person. Personal data which have undergone pseudonymisation, which could be attributed to a natural person by the use of additional information, should be considered to be information on an identifiable natural person.

GDPR Recital 32 - Consent Mechanisms: Consent should be given by a clear affirmative act establishing a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication. This could include ticking a box when visiting an internet website, choosing technical settings for information society services or another statement or conduct which clearly indicates acceptance.

GDPR Recital 39 - Transparency Principle: The principle of transparency requires that any information and communication relating to the processing of those personal data be easily accessible and easy to understand, and that clear and plain language be used. In particular, the specific purposes for which personal data are processed should be explicit and legitimate.

GDPR Recital 47 - Legitimate Interests Assessment: The legitimate interests of a controller, including those of a controller to which the personal data may be disclosed, or of a third party, may provide a legal basis for processing, provided that the interests or the fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject do not override those interests.

GDPR Recital 78 - Privacy by Design Principle: The protection of the rights and freedoms of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data requires that appropriate technical and organisational measures be taken to ensure that the requirements of this Regulation are met. In order to be able to demonstrate compliance, the controller should adopt internal policies.

GDPR Recital 83 - Security of Processing: In order to maintain security and to prevent processing in infringement of this Regulation, the controller or processor should evaluate the risks inherent in the processing and implement measures to mitigate those risks. These measures should ensure an appropriate level of security, taking into account the state of the art.

GDPR Recital 85 - Breach Notification Rationale: A personal data breach may, if not addressed in an appropriate and timely manner, result in physical, material or non-material damage to natural persons such as loss of control over their personal data, discrimination, identity theft or fraud, financial loss, or reputational damage.

GDPR Recital 113 - Transfers Without Adequate Decisions: Transfers should be possible where the data subject has given explicit consent, where the transfer is necessary to protect vital interests of the data subject or other persons where the data subject is unable to give consent, or where processing is necessary for public interest recognition.

GDPR Recital 148 - Penalties for Natural Persons: In order to strengthen the enforcement of the rules of this Regulation, penalties including administrative fines should be imposed for any infringement of this Regulation, in addition to appropriate measures imposed by the supervisory authority. Penalties may be imposed on natural persons not acting in a professional capacity.

CCPA Section 1798.100(a) - Notice at Collection: A business that collects a consumer's personal information shall, at or before the point of collection, inform consumers as to the categories of personal information to be collected and the purposes for which the categories of personal information shall be used. A business shall not collect additional categories of personal information without providing the consumer with notice.

CCPA Section 1798.100(b) - Right to Know: A business that collects a consumer's personal information shall, upon receipt of a verifiable consumer request, disclose to the consumer the categories and specific pieces of personal information the business has collected about that consumer.

CCPA Section 1798.100(c) - Right to Delete: A business that collects a consumer's personal information shall, upon receipt of a verifiable consumer request, delete the consumer's personal information from its records and direct any service providers to delete the consumer's personal information from their records.

CCPA Section 1798.100(d) - Right to Correct: A business that collects personal information about consumers shall, upon receipt of a verifiable consumer request, correct inaccurate personal information that a business maintains about a consumer. A business shall use commercially reasonable efforts to correct the inaccurate personal information.

CCPA Section 1798.105 - Right to Deletion: A consumer shall have the right to request that a business delete any personal information about the consumer which the business has collected from the consumer. A business that receives a verifiable consumer request shall delete the consumer's personal information from its records.

CCPA Section 1798.105(d) - Exceptions to Right to Delete: A business or a service provider shall not be required to comply with a consumer's request to delete the consumer's personal information if it is necessary to complete the transaction for which the personal information was collected, detect security incidents, comply with a legal obligation, or enable internal uses that are reasonably aligned with consumer expectations.

CCPA Section 1798.106 - Right to Correct Inaccurate Personal Information: A consumer shall have the right to request that a business that collects personal information about the consumer correct inaccurate personal information about the consumer, taking into account the nature of the personal information and the purposes of the processing.

CCPA Section 1798.110 - Right to Know Categories of Personal Information: A consumer shall have the right to request that a business that collects personal information about the consumer disclose to that consumer the categories of personal information it has collected, the sources from which the personal information is collected, and the business or commercial purpose for collecting or selling personal information.

CCPA Section 1798.110(c) - Disclosure of Third Parties: A business shall disclose to the consumer the categories of third parties with whom the business shares personal information and the categories of personal information that the business sold to or disclosed for a business purpose to third parties in the preceding 12 months.

CCPA Section 1798.115 - Right to Know About Disclosure for Business Purposes: A consumer shall have the right to request that a business that sells the consumer's personal information, or that discloses it for a business purpose, disclose to that consumer the categories of personal information that the business sold and the categories of personal information that the business disclosed for a business purpose.

CCPA Section 1798.120 - Right to Opt-Out of Sale: A consumer shall have the right, at any time, to direct a business that sells personal information about the consumer to third parties not to sell the consumer's personal information. A business shall not sell the personal information of consumers if the business has actual knowledge that the consumer is less than 16 years of age without affirmative authorisation.

CCPA Section 1798.120(b) - Under-13 Opt-In for Sale: A business shall not sell the personal information of a consumer who is less than 13 years of age unless the business has received affirmative authorisation from the consumer's parent or guardian. Violations involving minors are subject to enhanced penalties under the CCPA.

CCPA Section 1798.121 - Right to Limit Use of Sensitive Personal Information: A consumer shall have the right, at any time, to direct a business that collects sensitive personal information about the consumer to limit its use and disclosure of the consumer's sensitive personal information to use necessary to perform the services or provide the goods reasonably expected by an average consumer.

CCPA Section 1798.125 - Non-Discrimination: A business shall not discriminate against a consumer because the consumer exercised any of the consumer's rights under this title, including by denying goods or services, charging different prices or rates for goods or services, or providing a different level or quality of goods or services.

CCPA Section 1798.125(b) - Financial Incentives: A business may offer financial incentives, including payments to consumers as compensation, for the collection of personal information, the sale or sharing of personal information, or the retention of personal information. A business may also offer a different price or rate that is directly related to the value provided by the consumer's data.

CCPA Section 1798.130 - Methods of Submitting Requests: A business shall make available to consumers two or more designated methods for submitting requests for information required to be disclosed, including, at a minimum, a toll-free telephone number, and if the business maintains a website, a means to submit requests via the website.

CCPA Section 1798.130(a)(2) - Response Timeframe: A business shall respond to a verifiable consumer request within 45 days of receiving such a request. The business may extend this period once by an additional 45 days when reasonably necessary, provided the consumer is provided notice of the extension within the first 45-day period.

CCPA Section 1798.130(a)(3) - Free Response: A business shall provide information required by this section to a consumer free of charge. For requests that are manifestly unfounded or excessive, in particular because of their repetitive character, the business may either charge a reasonable fee or refuse to act on the request.

CCPA Section 1798.135 - Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information: A business that sells consumers' personal information to, or shares it with, third parties shall provide notice to consumers that this information may be sold or shared and that consumers have the right to opt out. The business shall include a clear and conspicuous link titled 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information' on the internet homepage.

CCPA Section 1798.135(b) - Global Opt-Out Signal: A business shall comply with an opt-out preference signal sent with the consumer's consent by a platform, technology, or mechanism to the business indicating the consumer's intent to opt out of the business's sale or sharing of the consumer's personal information. Businesses cannot penalise consumers who use such signals.

CCPA Section 1798.140(a) - Definition of Aggregate Consumer Information: Aggregate consumer information means information that relates to a group or category of consumers, from which individual consumer identities have been removed, that is not linked or reasonably linkable to any consumer or household, including via a device.

CCPA Section 1798.140(d) - Definition of Business: Business means a legal entity organised or operated for the profit or financial benefit of its shareholders or other owners that collects consumers' personal information, does business in California, and satisfies one or more thresholds including annual gross revenues exceeding $25 million.

CCPA Section 1798.140(g) - Definition of Consumer: Consumer means a natural person who is a California resident. The CCPA protects consumers in their capacity as consumers but also extends protection to individuals acting in a business-to-business context, covering employees, contractors, and job applicants.

CCPA Section 1798.140(l) - Definition of Personal Information: Personal information means information that identifies, relates to, describes, is reasonably capable of being associated with, or could reasonably be linked, directly or indirectly, with a particular consumer or household. It includes identifiers, commercial information, biometric data, internet activity, geolocation, and inferences.

CCPA Section 1798.140(ae) - Definition of Sensitive Personal Information: Sensitive personal information includes social security numbers, financial account information, precise geolocation, racial or ethnic origin, religious beliefs, union membership, the contents of mail, email and text messages, genetic data, biometric data used for unique identification, health information, and information concerning a consumer's sex life or sexual orientation.

CCPA Section 1798.140(ah) - Definition of Sale: Sale means selling, renting, releasing, disclosing, disseminating, making available, transferring, or otherwise communicating orally, in writing, or by electronic or other means, a consumer's personal information by the business to a third party for monetary or other valuable consideration.

CCPA Section 1798.140(aj) - Definition of Service Provider: Service provider means a sole proprietorship, partnership, limited liability company, corporation, association, or other legal entity organised or operated for the profit or financial benefit of its shareholders or other owners, that processes information on behalf of a business.

CCPA Section 1798.145(a) - Exemptions: The obligations of this title shall not restrict a business's ability to comply with federal, state, or local laws; comply with a civil, criminal, or regulatory inquiry, investigation, subpoena, or summons; or cooperate with law enforcement agencies concerning conduct or activity that the business reasonably and in good faith believes may violate federal, state, or local law.

CCPA Section 1798.145(c) - HIPAA Exemption: The obligations of this title shall not apply to protected health information that is collected by a covered entity or business associate governed by the privacy, security, and breach notification rules issued pursuant to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996.

CCPA Section 1798.145(d) - Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act Exemption: The obligations imposed on businesses by this title shall not apply to personal information collected, processed, sold, or disclosed pursuant to the federal Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and implementing regulations or the California Financial Information Privacy Act.

CCPA Section 1798.150(a) - Private Right of Action for Data Breach: Any consumer whose non-encrypted or non-redacted personal information is subject to an unauthorised access and exfiltration, theft, or disclosure as a result of the business's violation of the duty to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures may recover statutory damages between $100 and $750 per consumer per incident.

CCPA Section 1798.150(b) - Notice Before Private Action: A consumer bringing a private action shall provide a business 30 days' written notice before initiating an action. If within the 30 days the business cures the noticed violation and provides the consumer an express written statement that the violations have been cured, no action for damages may be initiated.

CCPA Section 1798.155 - Enforcement by Attorney General: Any business or third party that violates this title shall be liable for an injunction and be subject to a civil penalty of not more than $2,500 for each violation or $7,500 for each intentional violation or each violation involving the personal information of minor consumers.

CCPA Section 1798.155(b) - CPPA Enforcement: The California Privacy Protection Agency shall have the authority to investigate and prosecute violations of this title. The Agency may issue subpoenas, hold hearings, and impose administrative fines on businesses that violate the CCPA or its implementing regulations.

CCPA Section 1798.160 - Consumer Privacy Fund: There shall be established in the State Treasury the Consumer Privacy Fund, with the purpose of fully funding the costs of the establishment and ongoing operation of the California Privacy Protection Agency and the costs of the Attorney General in administering and enforcing this title.

CCPA Section 1798.175 - Conflicting Legislation: This title is intended to supplement federal and state law, where permissible, but shall not apply where such application is preempted by, or in conflict with, federal law or the United States or California Constitution. Businesses need not provide greater privacy rights where state or federal law requires disclosure.

CCPA Section 1798.180 - Preemption of Local Laws: This title is a matter of statewide concern and supersedes and preempts all rules, regulations, codes, ordinances, and other laws adopted by a city, county, city and county, municipality, or local agency regarding the collection and sale of consumers' personal information by a business.

CCPA Section 1798.185 - Regulations: The California Privacy Protection Agency shall promulgate regulations to further the purposes of this title, including establishing rules and procedures governing the following: the process for consumers to submit a request to a business to know about personal information the business has collected about that consumer.

CCPA Section 1798.185(a)(4) - Data Security Regulations: The Agency shall adopt regulations governing the security procedures and practices to protect the consumer's personal information from unauthorised access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure in accordance with Section 1798.81.5 of the Civil Code.

CCPA Section 1798.196 - Relationship to Other Laws: This title is not intended to conflict with and does not supersede, alter, or amend any other California privacy law, including the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act, the Information Practices Act of 1977, or the Online Privacy Protection Act.

CCPA Section 1798.199.10 - California Privacy Protection Agency: There is hereby established in state government the California Privacy Protection Agency, which is vested with full administrative power, authority, and jurisdiction to implement and enforce the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 and this title.

CCPA Section 1798.199.15 - Agency Board Members: The Agency shall be governed by a five-member board with the following qualifications: members shall include a privacy advocate, an expert in privacy law or technology, an expert in business, a member representing consumers, and a member representing civil rights groups.

CCPA Section 1798.199.25 - Agency Authority Over Businesses: The Agency may direct a business or service provider to produce any business records, business systems, or any other information relevant to any investigation of the business's compliance with this title. Failure to comply with Agency subpoenas may result in additional penalties.

CCPA Section 1798.199.40 - Agency Audit Authority: The Agency shall have authority to audit businesses and service providers to monitor for compliance with the CCPA. Audits may be announced or unannounced and shall be conducted in accordance with procedures established by the Agency.

CCPA Section 1798.199.45 - Investigative Process: Before the Agency initiates formal enforcement proceedings against a business, the Agency shall provide the business with notice of the alleged violation and an opportunity to cure the violation within 30 days, except where the violation involves the personal information of minor consumers.

CCPA Section 1798.199.55 - Right to Hearing: A person subject to an administrative enforcement proceeding before the Agency is entitled to a hearing before an independent administrative law judge. The person may present evidence and legal arguments, and the hearing record shall be the basis for the Agency's final decision.

CCPA Section 1798.199.85 - Judicial Review: Any person who has exhausted the administrative remedy provided in this title may obtain judicial review of a final decision of the Agency by filing a petition for a writ of mandamus in the court of appeal. Courts shall independently review questions of law and shall give substantial weight to factual findings.

CCPA Civil Code Section 1798.81.5 - Data Security: A business that owns, licenses, or maintains personal information about a California resident shall implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of the information, to protect the personal information from unauthorised access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure.

CCPA Civil Code Section 1798.82 - Security Breach Notification: A business that owns or licenses computerised data that includes personal information shall disclose any breach of the security of the system following discovery or notification of the breach in the security of the data to any California resident whose unencrypted personal information was acquired by an unauthorised person.

CCPA Civil Code Section 1798.82(f) - Breach Notification Timeframe: Any business that is required to issue a security breach notification shall do so in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, consistent with the legitimate needs of law enforcement or any measures necessary to determine the scope of the breach and restore the reasonable integrity of the data system.

CCPA Regulation 7001 - Purpose and Scope of Opt-Out Requests: Consumers have the right to opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal information. A business shall not sell or share a consumer's personal information after receiving the consumer's opt-out request, unless the consumer subsequently provides consent for such sale or sharing.

CCPA Regulation 7004 - Notice of Financial Incentive: If a business offers a financial incentive or price or service difference in exchange for the retention or sale of a consumer's personal information, it shall notify consumers of the financial incentive or price or service difference and shall obtain the consumer's prior opt-in consent.

CCPA Regulation 7011 - Privacy Policy Disclosures: A business's privacy policy shall include a description of consumers' rights under the CCPA including the right to know, the right to delete, the right to correct, the right to opt-out of sale or sharing, the right to limit use of sensitive personal information, and the right to non-discrimination.

CCPA Regulation 7012 - Annual Privacy Policy Update: A business shall review its privacy policy at least once every 12 months and update it to reflect any material changes in the business's personal information collection, use, or disclosure practices. The date the policy was last updated shall be clearly displayed in the policy.

CCPA Regulation 7020 - Verifiable Consumer Request Verification: A business shall establish, document, and comply with a reasonable method for verifying that the person making a verifiable consumer request is the consumer about whom the business has collected information, or is the consumer's authorised agent.

CCPA Regulation 7023 - Authorised Agent Verification: A business may require an authorised agent to provide proof of authorisation to act on the consumer's behalf. A business shall not require a consumer to directly verify the request or provide information beyond what is necessary when the consumer has provided a power of attorney to the agent.

CCPA Regulation 7025 - Household Requests: If a business receives a request to know or delete from a consumer who is a member of a household, the business may respond to such request by providing the personal information for that individual consumer and shall not require the consent of other members of the household to provide individual information.

CCPA Regulation 7026 - Service Provider and Contractor Restrictions: A service provider or contractor shall not retain, use, or disclose personal information obtained in the course of providing services to a business for any purpose other than for the specific purpose of performing the services specified in the contract with the business.

CCPA Regulation 7027 - Contracts with Service Providers: A business that transfers personal information to a service provider or contractor for a business purpose shall enter into a written contract that prohibits the service provider or contractor from selling or sharing the personal information, retaining or using the personal information outside of the direct business relationship, or combining personal information received from a business with personal information received from other sources.

CCPA Regulation 7040 - Dark Patterns Prohibition: A business shall not use a dark pattern to obtain consent or to make it more difficult for a consumer to exercise their rights. A dark pattern means a user interface that has the substantial effect of subverting or impairing user autonomy, decision-making, or choice.

CCPA Regulation 7050 - Data Minimisation for Sensitive Personal Information: A business that collects sensitive personal information shall limit the collection of sensitive personal information to what is reasonably necessary and proportionate to achieve the purposes for which it was collected or processed, or for another disclosed purpose.

CCPA Regulation 7051 - Purpose Limitation for Sensitive Personal Information: A business shall not use or disclose sensitive personal information collected pursuant to the limit on use and disclosure for any purpose other than to provide the goods or services requested by the consumer, or for other limited purposes as defined in the regulations.

CCPA Regulation 7060 - Risk Assessments: A business that processes personal information that presents significant risk to consumers' privacy or security shall conduct risk assessments on a regular basis. The risk assessment shall identify and assess the safeguards the business has implemented to address the identified risks to consumers.

CCPA Regulation 7070 - Automated Decision-Making Technology: Businesses that use automated decision-making technology in ways that are subject to the right to opt-out shall provide consumers with the right to opt out of the business's use of automated decision-making technology including profiling for decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects.

CCPA Regulation 7071 - Right to Access Automated Decision Logic: Consumers who are subject to a decision or significant prediction, recommendation, or classification made by automated decision-making technology shall have the right to obtain meaningful information about the logic involved in that decision-making process.

CCPA Regulation 7080 - Cybersecurity Audit Requirements: Businesses that process consumers' personal information that presents significant risk to consumers' security shall conduct a cybersecurity audit on an annual basis. The cybersecurity audit shall be performed by a qualified, objective, and independent professional.

CCPA Regulation 7100 - Children's Personal Information: A business that operates websites or online services directed at children or has actual knowledge that it is collecting personal information from a child under 13 years of age shall not sell or share the personal information of the child, and must obtain affirmative authorisation from the child's parent or guardian before doing so.

CCPA Regulation 7101 - Minors Between 13 and 16: A business that has actual knowledge that it is collecting personal information of a consumer between 13 and 16 years of age shall not sell or share the personal information of the consumer unless the consumer affirmatively authorises the sale or sharing of their personal information.

GDPR Article 4(5) - Definition of Pseudonymisation: Pseudonymisation means the processing of personal data in such a manner that the personal data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and is subject to technical and organisational measures.

GDPR Article 4(12) - Definition of Personal Data Breach: Personal data breach means a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data transmitted, stored or otherwise processed. Even temporary loss of access to data may constitute a breach if it causes harm.

GDPR Article 4(13) - Definition of Genetic Data: Genetic data means personal data relating to the inherited or acquired genetic characteristics of a natural person which give unique information about the physiology or the health of that natural person and which result, in particular, from an analysis of a biological sample from the natural person in question.

GDPR Article 4(14) - Definition of Biometric Data: Biometric data means personal data resulting from specific technical processing relating to the physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics of a natural person, which allow or confirm the unique identification of that natural person, such as facial images or dactyloscopic data.

GDPR Article 4(15) - Definition of Health Data: Data concerning health means personal data related to the physical or mental health of a natural person, including the provision of health care services, which reveal information about his or her health status. This includes information collected during registration for and provision of health care services.

GDPR Article 4(22) - Definition of Supervisory Authority: Supervisory authority means an independent public authority established by a Member State pursuant to Article 51. Each supervisory authority must be fully independent in the exercise of its tasks and powers and each member shall abstain from any action incompatible with their duties.

GDPR Article 56 - Competence of the Lead Supervisory Authority: Where a controller or processor is established in more than one Member State, the supervisory authority of the main establishment or of the single establishment of the controller or processor shall be competent to act as lead supervisory authority for cross-border processing.

GDPR Article 61 - Mutual Assistance: Supervisory authorities shall provide each other with relevant information and mutual assistance in order to implement and apply this Regulation in a consistent manner, and shall put in place measures for effective cooperation with one another. This cooperation shall include requests for information, supervisory measures, and enforcement activities.

GDPR Article 62 - Joint Operations: Supervisory authorities shall, where appropriate, conduct joint operations including joint investigations and joint enforcement measures with the participation of members or staff of supervisory authorities of other Member States in activities carried out in their territory.

GDPR Article 63 - Consistency Mechanism: In order to contribute to the consistent application of this Regulation throughout the Union, the supervisory authorities shall cooperate with each other and, where relevant, with the Commission through the consistency mechanism as established in this Chapter.

GDPR Article 64 - Opinion of the Board: The Board shall issue an opinion where a supervisory authority intends to adopt a list of processing operations subject to the requirement for a data protection impact assessment, or where a supervisory authority intends to approve standard contractual clauses.

GDPR Article 66 - Urgency Procedure: In exceptional circumstances, where a supervisory authority considers that there is an urgent need to act in order to protect the rights and freedoms of data subjects, it may immediately adopt provisional measures with a specified period of validity of no longer than three months.

GDPR Article 68 - European Data Protection Board: The European Data Protection Board is established as a body of the Union and shall have legal personality. The Board shall ensure consistent application of the Regulation and shall consist of the head of one supervisory authority of each Member State and the European Data Protection Supervisor.

GDPR Article 69 - Independence of the Board: The Board shall act independently when performing its tasks or exercising its powers. In the performance of its tasks, the Board shall neither seek nor take instructions from anybody. This independence shall not preclude consultation and cooperation with other Union institutions as appropriate.

GDPR Article 70 - Tasks of the Board: The Board shall ensure the consistent application of this Regulation. It shall issue guidelines and recommendations on data protection matters, promote cooperation between supervisory authorities, publish opinions on draft decisions of lead supervisory authorities, and promote standard contractual clauses.

GDPR Article 75 - Rules of Procedure of the Board: The Board shall determine its own rules of procedure by a simple majority of its members. The secretariat shall be provided by the European Data Protection Supervisor. The Board's secretariat shall perform its tasks exclusively under the instructions of the Chair of the Board.

GDPR Article 76 - Confidentiality of Board Proceedings: The discussions of the Board shall be confidential where the Board deems it necessary as provided for in its rules of procedure. Access to documents submitted to members of the Board, experts and representatives of third parties shall be governed by Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001.

CCPA Civil Code Section 1798.83 - Shine the Light Law: A business subject to Section 17 that discloses a customer's personal information to third parties for those third parties' direct marketing purposes shall, upon written or electronic request, provide to that customer information about that disclosure free of charge within 30 days.

CCPA Civil Code Section 1798.90 - Online Tracking Technologies: A business that operates websites or online services shall disclose what personal information it collects through online tracking technologies, including cookies, pixel tags, and browser fingerprinting, and provide consumers with the ability to opt out from such tracking.

CCPA Section 1798.100(e) - Right to Data Portability: A business that maintains personal information about a consumer shall provide the consumer, upon a verifiable consumer request, with personal information in a portable, and to the extent technically feasible, readily usable format that allows the consumer to transmit this information to another entity.

CCPA Regulation 7200 - Minimum Security Standards: Businesses processing sensitive personal information shall implement and document administrative, physical, and technical safeguards including access controls, encryption of data in transit and at rest, regular security testing, and employee training on data handling requirements.

CCPA Regulation 7202 - Incident Response Plans: Businesses subject to the CCPA shall maintain a documented data breach incident response plan that identifies key personnel responsible for responding to breaches, procedures for identifying and assessing breaches, notification procedures, and remediation steps.

GDPR Recital 4 - Right to Protection of Personal Data: The processing of personal data should be designed to serve mankind. The right to the protection of personal data is not an absolute right; it must be considered in relation to its function in society and be balanced against other fundamental rights, in accordance with the principle of proportionality.

GDPR Recital 6 - Technology and Globalisation Challenges: Rapid technological developments and globalisation have brought new challenges for the protection of personal data. The scale of the collection and sharing of personal data has increased significantly. Technology allows personal data to be shared and used to an unprecedented degree.

GDPR Recital 14 - Protection Regardless of Nationality: The protection afforded by this Regulation should apply to natural persons, whatever their nationality or place of residence, in relation to the processing of their personal data. This Regulation does not cover the processing of personal data which concerns legal persons.

GDPR Recital 23 - Applicable to Non-EU Controllers: Processing by a controller not established in the Union should be subject to this Regulation when the processing activities are related to the offering of goods or services to such data subjects irrespective of whether a payment of the data subject is required.

GDPR Recital 40 - Lawfulness of Processing: For processing to be lawful, personal data should be processed on the basis of the consent of the data subject concerned or some other legitimate basis, laid down by law, either in this Regulation or in other Union or Member State law as referred to in this Regulation.

GDPR Recital 50 - Further Processing Compatibility: Processing of personal data for purposes other than those for which the personal data were initially collected should be allowed only where the processing is compatible with the purposes for which the personal data were initially collected. The controller should bear responsibility for compatibility of further processing.

GDPR Recital 58 - Transparency Principle Application: The principle of transparency requires that any information addressed to the public or to the data subject be concise, easily accessible and easy to understand, and that clear and plain language and, additionally, where appropriate, visualisation is used.

GDPR Recital 60 - Information Obligations: The principles of fair and transparent processing require that the data subject be informed of the existence of the processing operation and its purposes. The controller should provide the data subject with any further information necessary to ensure fair and transparent processing.

GDPR Recital 65 - Right to Erasure Rationale: A data subject should have the right to have personal data erased and no longer processed where the personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are collected or otherwise processed, where a data subject has withdrawn their consent, or where the data subject objects to the processing.

GDPR Recital 71 - Automated Decision-Making Safeguards: The data subject should have the right not to be subject to a decision, which may include a measure, evaluating personal aspects relating to him or her which is based solely on automated processing and which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her.

GDPR Recital 74 - Accountability of Controllers: The responsibility and liability of the controller for any processing of personal data carried out by the controller or on the controller's behalf should be established. In particular, the controller should be obliged to implement appropriate and effective measures and be able to demonstrate the compliance.

GDPR Recital 75 - Risks to Rights and Freedoms: The risks to the rights and freedoms of natural persons may result from personal data processing which could lead to physical, material or non-material damage, in particular: where the processing may give rise to discrimination, identity theft or fraud, financial loss, damage to the reputation, or significant economic or social disadvantage.

GDPR Recital 100 - Data Protection Officer Role: In order to strengthen compliance with this Regulation, controllers or processors whose core activities consist of processing operations that require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale, or of special categories of data, should be assisted by a person with expert knowledge of data protection law.

GDPR Recital 101 - International Data Transfers Rationale: Flows of personal data to and from countries outside the Union and international organisations are necessary for the expansion of international trade and international cooperation. The increase in such flows has raised new challenges and concerns with regard to the protection of personal data.

GDPR Recital 103 - Adequacy Decisions: The Commission may decide with effect for the entire Union that a third country, a territory or specified sector within a third country, or an international organisation, offers an adequate level of data protection, thereby providing legal certainty and uniformity throughout the Union.

GDPR Recital 111 - Standard Contractual Clauses: The controller or processor should be encouraged to provide further safeguards via contractual commitments that supplement standard protection clauses adopted by a supervisory authority or by the Commission. Standard contractual clauses are recognised as an appropriate safeguard for data transfers.

GDPR Recital 129 - Investigative Powers of Supervisory Authorities: In order to fulfil their mission of monitoring and enforcing the application of this Regulation, supervisory authorities should have the necessary powers, including investigative powers such as the power to access documents and to carry out on-site data protection audits.

GDPR Recital 150 - Fines as Effective Deterrence: Administrative fines can be effective in achieving the goal of deterrence. In order to strengthen the enforcement of the rules of this Regulation, penalties including administrative fines should be imposed for any infringement of this Regulation, in addition to, or instead of appropriate measures imposed by the supervisory authority.

CCPA Section 1798.100(f) - Retention Schedule Disclosure: A business shall disclose to consumers the length of time it intends to retain each category of sensitive personal information, or if that is not possible, the criteria used to determine that period. Indefinite retention without justification violates the spirit of data minimisation.

CCPA Regulation 7002 - Processing of Opt-Out Requests: A business shall act on a consumer's opt-out request as soon as feasibly possible, but no later than 15 business days from the date the business receives the consumer's request. The business shall also send a signal to all third parties to whom it has sold or shared personal information within 90 days.

CCPA Regulation 7003 - Do Not Sell or Share Button Implementation: A business shall implement and maintain a conspicuous link on its internet homepage titled 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information'. The link shall be in a colour that contrasts with the background colour of the page and shall be clearly distinguishable from the surrounding text.

CCPA Regulation 7005 - Methods for Submitting Deletion Requests: A business shall provide at least two methods for consumers to submit deletion requests: a toll-free telephone number and a website form or email address. Businesses operating exclusively online need only provide an email address for submission of requests.

CCPA Regulation 7006 - Two-Step Deletion Process: For deletion requests submitted online, a business may use a two-step process that requires the consumer to first submit the request and then separately confirm the request. The business shall not require more than two steps and the process shall be easy for consumers to use.

CCPA Regulation 7007 - Processing of Correction Requests: A business shall use commercially reasonable efforts to correct inaccurate personal information as directed by the consumer. When a consumer submits a correction request, the business shall review the request and either correct the inaccurate personal information or respond with the reason it cannot comply with the request.

CCPA Regulation 7008 - Retention of Records of Consumer Requests: A business shall maintain records of consumer requests made pursuant to this title and how the business responded to such requests for a period of 24 months. Records shall include the date the request was received, the nature of the request, the manner in which the request was fulfilled, and the date of the business's response.

CCPA Regulation 7010 - Notices to Consumers: A business shall provide privacy information to consumers at collection and in a privacy policy. Notices shall be written in plain, straightforward language and avoid technical or legal jargon. Notices shall be in the same languages in which the business provides goods and services to consumers.

GDPR Article 11 - Processing Which Does Not Require Identification: If the purposes for which a controller processes personal data do not or do no longer require the identification of a data subject by the controller, the controller shall not be obliged to maintain, acquire or process additional information in order to identify the data subject.

GDPR Article 41 - Monitoring of Approved Codes of Conduct: Without prejudice to the tasks and powers of the competent supervisory authority, the monitoring of compliance with a code of conduct may be carried out by a body which has an appropriate level of expertise in relation to the subject-matter of the code and is accredited for that purpose.

GDPR Article 43 - Certification Bodies: Without prejudice to the tasks and powers of the competent supervisory authority, certification bodies which have an appropriate level of expertise in relation to data protection shall issue and renew certification after informing the supervisory authority of such certification in order to allow for monitoring.

GDPR Article 50 - International Cooperation: The Commission and supervisory authorities shall take appropriate steps to develop international cooperation mechanisms to facilitate the effective enforcement of legislation for the protection of personal data, and to provide international mutual assistance in the enforcement of legislation for the protection of personal data.

GDPR Article 53 - General Conditions for Members of Supervisory Authorities: Member States shall provide for each member of their supervisory authorities to be appointed by means of a transparent procedure by their parliament, government or head of state. Each member shall have the qualifications, experience and skills required to perform their duties.

GDPR Article 54 - Rules on Establishment of Supervisory Authority: Each Member State shall provide by law for the establishment of each supervisory authority, including the conditions for appointment of members, rules and procedures applicable to members, and general rules applicable to the supervisory authority, including adequate financial and staff resources.

GDPR Article 59 - Activity Reports of Supervisory Authorities: Each supervisory authority shall draw up an annual report on its activity, which may include a list of types of infringement notified and types of measures taken. Those reports shall be transmitted to the national parliament, the government and other authorities as designated by Member State law.

CCPA Section 1798.140(c) - Definition of Biometric Information: Biometric information includes an individual's physiological, biological, or behavioural characteristics that can be used, singly or in combination with each other or with other identifying data, to establish individual identity, including fingerprints, retina and iris patterns, voice prints, and gait patterns.

CCPA Section 1798.140(h) - Definition of Deidentified Information: Deidentified means information that cannot reasonably identify, relate to, describe, be capable of being associated with, or be linked, directly or indirectly, to a particular consumer, provided that a business that uses deidentified information implements technical safeguards and business processes that prohibit reidentification.

CCPA Section 1798.140(i) - Definition of Designated Methods for Submitting Requests: Designated methods for submitting requests means a mailing address, email address, internet website form, internet website page, internet-based service, internet application, or other applicable contact information, whereby consumers may submit a request or direction under this title.

CCPA Section 1798.140(n) - Definition of Profiling: Profiling means any form of automated processing of personal information to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person and, in particular, to analyse or predict aspects concerning that natural person's performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences, interests, reliability, or location.

CCPA Section 1798.140(t) - Definition of Sharing: Share means sharing, renting, releasing, disclosing, disseminating, making available, transferring, or otherwise communicating orally, in writing, or by electronic or other means, a consumer's personal information by the business to a third party for cross-context behavioural advertising.

CCPA Section 1798.140(v) - Definition of Third Party: Third party means a person who is not the business that collects personal information from consumers under this title, or a service provider or contractor to whom the business discloses a consumer's personal information for a business purpose pursuant to a written contract.
